### 2025 Enderlin tornado

The 2025 Enderlin tornado was an intense, multiple-vortex tornado that struck rural areas near Enderlin in southeastern North Dakota during the late evening of June 20, 2025. Rated EF5 on the Enhanced Fujita scale with estimated peak wind speeds exceeding 210 miles per hour (340 km/h), it was the first tornado in the United States to receive this rating since the 2013 Moore tornado in Oklahoma. The tornado caused three fatalities, destroyed multiple farm structures, derailed dozens of train cars, and inflicted severe damage to vegetation and cropland along a 12.1-mile-long (19.5 km) path. Initially rated EF3 by the National Weather Service, it was upgraded to EF5 on October 6, 2025, following additional surveys and physics-based analysis of damage indicators. 

The event occurred amid a broader severe weather outbreak from June 19 to 22, 2025, which produced 41 confirmed tornadoes across the Northern Plains, driven by supercell thunderstorms ahead of an advancing derecho. The Enderlin tornado's rapid intensification, evidenced by radar data showing a doubling of rotational velocity in under six minutes, highlighted the storm's explosive development. While the tornado's rural path limited the number of affected structures, the severity of observed damage—such as the lofting of heavy rail equipment and cycloidal ground scouring—supported the high rating. Recovery efforts included federal disaster assistance, with North Dakota Governor Kelly Armstrong securing FEMA funding to aid rebuilding in impacted communities. 

#### Meteorological history
On June 20, 2025, a shortwave trough and associated upper-level jet stream contributed to unstable atmospheric conditions across the Northern Plains. Supercell thunderstorms developed in southeast North Dakota during the evening hours, fueled by high convective available potential energy (CAPE) and strong deep-layer shear. These storms produced several tornadoes, including an EF2 in Enderlin itself and others rated up to EF3 nearby. 

The Enderlin tornado touched down at 11:02 p.m. CDT (04:02 UTC June 21) approximately 3 miles (4.8 km) southwest of Enderlin in Ransom County. Radar from the NWS Grand Forks office indicated initial rotational velocity (VROT) of 53 knots, which surged to 106 knots by 11:08 p.m., signaling rapid strengthening. The tornado moved east-northeast at around 35 mph (56 km/h), expanding to a maximum width of 1 mile (1.6 km) as it crossed farmland and the Maple River. It exhibited multiple vortices, with cycloidal marks in fields confirming intense ground-level winds. 

The storm's mesocyclone, visible on radar and captured by chasers, persisted as the tornado lifted near Alice at 11:21 p.m. CDT. Following the tornadoes, a derecho with gusts over 100 mph (160 km/h) traversed the state, exacerbating damage from downed trees and power lines. A mesoscale convective vortex prolonged high winds for several hours afterward. 

#### Preparations and warnings
The Storm Prediction Center issued a moderate risk outlook for severe weather on June 20, highlighting the potential for strong tornadoes in southeast North Dakota. Tornado watches were in effect by early evening, with warnings issued as radar detected rotation. Local NWS offices, spotters, and storm chasers provided real-time reports, aiding in timely alerts. Despite the nighttime occurrence, which reduced visibility, warnings reached rural residents via emergency broadcasts and mobile alerts. 

#### Impact
The tornado's path primarily affected agricultural areas, resulting in catastrophic damage to farms and infrastructure. A key damage indicator was the derailment of 33 train cars on a Burlington Northern Santa Fe line south of Enderlin, including loaded grain hoppers weighing up to 286,000 pounds (130 metric tons) rolled or thrown up to 475 feet (145 m). Physics-based models estimated winds of 230 mph (370 km/h) for hopper displacement and up to 266 mph (428 km/h) for a lighter tanker car. 

Farmsteads were completely scoured, with foundations swept clean and debris scattered over miles. Vegetation damage included debarking of trees along the Maple River, with a "sandpapering" effect on bark, and ground scouring that tilled corn fields 12–18 inches (30–46 cm) deep across a 1-mile swath. Three people died in collapsed structures, though the rural setting limited broader casualties. Economic losses included destroyed crops, equipment, and rail disruptions. 

| Damage Indicator | Estimated Wind Speed (mph) | Description |
|------------------|----------------------------|-------------|
| Train Hopper Derailment | ~230 | Loaded cars rolled or thrown |
| Tanker Car Displacement | ~266 | 72,000-lb car lofted 475 ft |
| Tree Debarking | 167+ | Sandpapering effect on bark |
| Farmstead Scouring | 200+ | Foundations swept clean |
| Ground Scouring | 210+ | Corn fields tilled deeply |

The broader outbreak's derecho caused additional wind damage, with gusts up to 111 mph elsewhere in the state. 

#### Aftermath
North Dakota Governor Kelly Armstrong declared a statewide disaster on June 21, 2025, citing the storm's widespread impact. In September, President Joseph R. Biden Jr. approved federal disaster assistance through FEMA, providing funds for infrastructure repairs and individual aid. Over 150 volunteers assisted in debris removal from fields, using drones to locate scattered items. The Enderlin Area Tornado Relief Fund, managed by BankNorth, supported rebuilding, though challenges arose from inadequate insurance coverage. Mental health services were offered to survivors. 

The EF5 upgrade prompted discussions on refining the Enhanced Fujita scale for non-structural indicators, with comparisons to international tornado ratings. Storm chasers' footage and analyses, including cycloidal coefficient methods, corroborated the intensity.

**Overview**

***** This page will continue to be updated periodically as new information is gathered.*****

During the evening and overnight of Friday, June 20 th, much of the region was affected by severe weather. Supercell thunderstorms developed across southeast North Dakota ahead of an approaching convective complex, producing multiple strong, destructive, and fatal tornadoes. This was followed by a powerful line of severe thunderstorms known as a "[derecho](http://www.spc.noaa.gov/misc/AbtDerechos/derechofaq.htm)", which tracked across much of the region resulting in widespread straight line wind damage. After the derecho passed through the region, there was a period of prolonged destructive winds that affected portions of central and east central North Dakota, as well as adjacent portions of Minnesota.

This was a unique event due to the combination of the violent tornadoes ahead of the derecho, and the long duration of significant winds that followed the derecho.

**Tornadic Supercell Thunderstorms**

Tornadic supercell thunderstorms developed across southeast North Dakota during the evening hours, leading to several tornadoes.

**Derecho**

The derecho portion of this severe event tracked from west to east across North Dakota during the evening hours, with widespread wind gusts over 60 mph, with some locations gusting over 100 mph. As the derecho moved into eastern North Dakota, it caught up with the tornadic supercell storms. The northern portion of the derecho weakened as it moved into Minnesota, but the southern portion regained strength and moved across portions of Minnesota through the early morning hours. Extensive damage was reported, especially in areas that gusted over 100 mph.

*   [Significant Damage around Bemidji](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=PNSFGF&e=202506271801)

**Significant Post Derecho Winds**

After the derecho passed, a portion of the region had to deal with a 2 to 3 hour period of 60-100+mph winds, leading to extensive damage across this portion of the region. These significant post derecho winds were caused by a m**esoscale convective vortex(MCV). MCVs are compact circulations in the atmosphere that happen in the wake of convective complexes.**A prolonged period of increased wind can occur at the tip of the MCV. S****trong convective complexes, like derechos, typically lead to more intense MCVs, which can lead to very strong winds.********

North Dakota’s tornado changed EF rate
======================================

[Josephine Lau](https://theticker.org/staff_name/josephine-lau/), Copy Chief

December 8, 2025

[![Image 11: NWS Fort Worth I Wikimedia Commons](https://theticker.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/NWS-FORT-WORTH-I-WIKIMEDIA-COMMONS.jpg)](https://theticker.org/17689/science/2025-enderlin-tornado-upgraded-marking-u-s-s-first-ef5-in-12-years/#photo)

NWS Fort Worth I Wikimedia Commons

A tornado that touched down near Enderlin, N.D., on June 20, was [upgraded](https://www.weather.gov/media/fgf/Enderlin.pdf) to a rating EF5 on the Enhanced Fujita scale, making it the first tornado since May 2013 to receive the rating.

The tornado, lasting 19 minutes with a 12-mile path, was part of a derecho — a widespread, long-lasting windstorm that accompanied several fast-moving thunderstorms or showers — that caused 41 tornadoes during the tornado outbreak from June 19 to June 22.

The tornado was initially rated EF3 by the National Weather Service in Grand Forks, N.D., but the rating was upgraded in October following a revised survey of the tornado’s damage.

The revised survey was conducted by Tim Marshall, Jim LaDue, Connell Miller, Greg Kopp, David Sills and the Northern Tornadoes Project at the Canadian Severe Storms Laboratory of Western University.

Most notably, the survey found that 33 derailed train cars weighing between 72,000 pounds and 286,000 pounds were thrown and landed nearly 500 feet from each other because of the tornado. Researchers and meteorologists found that “analyses estimate potential wind speeds of approximately 230 mph are needed to completely overturn a fully loaded grain hopper car,” [The Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/weather/2025/10/11/north-dakota-tornado-ef5-rare-rating/) reports.

The [EF Scale](https://www.weather.gov/oun/efscale), operational since February 2007, is derived from the[Fujita Scale](https://www.weather.gov/ffc/fujita). Its estimated wind speed ranges are based on damage from the tornado. Ratings, which are given from levels zero to five, are assigned based on the highest wind speed that occurred on the tornado’s path.

The previous EF5 tornado prior to the “EF5 drought” in the U.S. was the 2013 Moore tornado, which occurred in Oklahoma.

The tornado caused three casualties and zero injuries. North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong declared a statewide disaster on June 21 following the tornado. A month later, he made a request for a presidential disaster declaration for the damage dealt by the storms and tornados; the request was [approved](https://www.governor.nd.gov/news/president-trump-grants-armstrongs-request-major-disaster-declaration-severe-storm-damage-june) in September.

The approval would allow access to the Federal Emergency Management Agency funds.

“This much-needed disaster aid will help our state’s communities and utilities recover from one of the most powerful summer storms in recent history,” Armstrong said.

Days after the tornado, over 150 volunteers from different counties in the state [helped](https://www.agweek.com/weather/we-all-come-together-over-150-volunteers-clean-up-enderlin-farms-after-deadly-tornadoes) clean debris from farm fields in Enderlin. Drones were also used to search for missing belongings from damaged houses.

The town will continue rebuilding in the months following the tornado. In fact, mental health services and funds, such as the [Enderlin Area Tornado Relief Fund](https://www.wdayradionow.com/news/local-news/local-bank-sets-up-fund-for-enderlin-tornado-victims/) Relief Fund from BankNorth, have been set up for families affected by the storms, including the tornado.

Still, “people don’t realize what it costs to rebuild or they thought their insurance had something, but then they realize it wasn’t what they thought it said it was,” Maggie Peters from the Enderlin Area Tornado Relief Fund [said](https://www.inforum.com/news/north-dakota/fargo-fashion-show-set-to-help-enderlin-tornado-victims).
